A close reading for the week

“the White Way of Delight”

Anne of Green Gables · Chapter II

A shy man is driving an orphan he did not ask for home to a farm that wanted a boy. On the way she renames everything she sees, and what looks like a child’s chatter is the book’s argument about how to survive a hard life.

“Oh, it was wonderful—wonderful. It’s the first thing I ever saw that couldn’t be improved upon by imagination. It just satisfied me here”—she put one hand on her breast—“it made a queer funny ache and yet it was a pleasant ache.”1

“But they shouldn’t call that lovely place the Avenue. There is no meaning in a name like that. They should call it—let me see—the White Way of Delight.2 Isn’t that a nice imaginative name?

  1. 1

    Beauty felt as a bodily ache

    Anne locates joy physically, with a hand on her breast: “a queer funny ache and yet… a pleasant ache”. The oxymoron is exact childhood: intense beauty registers as something close to pain. And the Avenue is “the first thing I ever saw that couldn’t be improved upon by imagination”, a startling admission from a child who improves everything, and the book’s first hint of how much of her world she has had to make up because the real one gave her so little.

  2. 2

    Renaming as re-making

    “The Avenue” is dismissed (“there is no meaning in a name like that”) and replaced with “the White Way of Delight”. Anne takes possession of the place by naming it, as Adam named the animals. Naming is her form of power, the one kind available to a penniless orphan: she cannot own anything, but she can rechristen the whole visible world and make it hers.
